sourceText: The BRIN-UPLIFT-COMMONS sector was already in progress when they entered. For several lessons Aster had refused to pause worlds for their arrival; the fact that a class was visiting was not a cosmic event for the inhabitants. A species is given accelerated intelligence, but the uplift contract requires millennia of service to its patrons. The memorial bore the name of David Brin — Uplift precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Biology had to be treated as political infrastructure. A body capable of breathing another atmosphere, not aging, or sharing a mind with another species immediately produces new classes of obligation and new definitions of personhood. Tern had specialized in things that did not answer. In a family built for exploration, he had become the custodian of the right to silence. Darin was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Darin had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional pedagogy; there was a local problem, with deadlines, relatives, and consequences. For Darin, the speculative mechanism was not an 141 ‘idea.’ It was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing. The problem closed quickly around them: A young uplifted being asks whether he owes gratitude for the existence of a version of himself that nobody asked him to become. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Up — Uplift: a species is technologically raised to intelligence; Pc — Planetary Computer: an entire world becomes a computational substrate. Course references included David Brin — Uplift; computronium traditions. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Orin broke the first consensus. ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ Marae answered without raising their voice: ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. The White Hunger appeared in Aster as a loss of relief. She did not lack entertainment. She lacked the resistance of things to the model. When she could anticipate every reaction, the world became 142 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS functionally an extension of her own mind, and the presence of the other thinned toward simulacrum. Vela evaluated the solution not by efficiency but by the differences it made invisible. She found one: a local minority for whom the proposed “improvement” destroyed a practice with no equivalent. Optimizing the average concealed a small and perfectly legal extinction. The night did not end in victory. Aster avoids Tern's gaze because the question also describes their relationship. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. While Kesh closed the record, Tern compared the sector’s noise with the anomaly detected in the Vinge zone. The pattern reappeared, but only in worlds where Aster’s control weakened. The correlation was unpleasant: either someone was calling him from outside, or his own need for an outside was learning to forge evidence. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the INVERSION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — reverses an order, dependence, direction, or relation taken as natural — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 143 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. They left without an oral summary. Aster had abandoned the habit of closing every night with a thesis; some worlds were more honestly preserved as problems than as lessons. 144 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
